note: Starter corpus for Day 2 — a small, hand-written set of standard first-aid/disaster-response guidance, not the full NDMA/IFRC/WHO/Sphere corpus the PRD describes (docs/PRD.md §6.2). See docs/adr/0009-on-device-assistant-scope.md for what's real here vs. what Day 3 replaces it with.

chunks.text: For severe bleeding: apply firm, direct pressure to the wound with the cleanest cloth available and do not remove it once soaked — add more layers on top instead. Raise the injured area above heart level if possible. Do not apply a tourniquet unless bleeding is life-threatening and pressure has failed, and only if you know how — an incorrectly applied tourniquet can cause more harm. Keep the person still, warm, and calm. Get them to a hospital or call emergency services (112) as soon as possible.

chunks.source: Standard first-aid guidance (WHO snakebite guidance style)
chunks.text: For a snake bite: keep the person as still and calm as possible — movement speeds venom spread. Remove any tight clothing, rings, or jewellery near the bite before swelling starts. Keep the bitten limb below heart level. Do NOT cut the wound, do NOT try to suck out venom, do NOT apply ice, and do NOT apply a tight tourniquet — these are outdated and can cause serious harm. A firm (not tight) pressure bandage over the bite, if you know how to apply one, can help. Get to a hospital immediately — antivenom is the only real treatment. Call 112.

chunks.source: Standard first-aid guidance (CPR/basic life support style)
chunks.text: If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally: call for help and 112 immediately, then start chest compressions. Push hard and fast in the center of the chest, at least 5 cm deep, at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute — roughly two per second. Let the chest fully rise between compressions. Continue until emergency help arrives or the person starts breathing normally. If you are trained in rescue breaths, give 30 compressions then 2 breaths and repeat; if untrained, continuous hands-only compressions are still effective and recommended.

During a flood: move to higher ground immediately, do not wait for water to rise further. Never walk, swim, or drive through moving flood water — just 15 cm of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet, and 30 cm can carry away a car. Avoid contact with flood water where possible — it may be contaminated or electrically live from downed power lines. Keep important documents and a phone in a sealed waterproof bag. If trapped in a building, move to the highest level but not a closed attic where you could be trapped by rising water. Signal for help from a window or roof.

During an earthquake: Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Drop to your hands and knees, take cover under a sturdy table or desk if available, and hold on until the shaking stops. Stay away from windows, mirrors, and heavy furniture that could fall. If outdoors, move to an open area away from buildings, trees, and power lines. If in a vehicle, stop safely away from overpasses and bridges and stay inside. After shaking stops, expect aftershocks, check for injuries and hazards like gas leaks, and evacuate a damaged building if it's unsafe. Landslides can follow earthquakes on unstable slopes — move away from steep slopes if you feel or hear ground movement.

Signs of shock include pale, cold, clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, rapid breathing, and confusion or dizziness. Lay the person down and raise their legs about 30 cm unless a leg injury or breathing difficulty makes this uncomfortable. Keep them warm with a blanket or coat. Do not give food or water in case they need surgery. Loosen tight clothing. Monitor breathing and pulse, and get emergency help — shock can be life-threatening on its own, separate from the original injury.

For a burn: cool the area under cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 20 minutes as soon as possible. Remove jewellery or tight clothing near the burn before swelling starts, but do not remove clothing that is stuck to the skin. Do not apply ice, butter, oil, or toothpaste — these can worsen the injury. Cover loosely with clean, non-fluffy cloth or cling film. Seek medical attention for burns larger than the person's palm, burns on the face/hands/genitals, or burns that look white or charred.

When told to evacuate: go immediately, do not wait to gather non-essential belongings. Take a torch, phone, any medicines you need, important documents, and water if you can carry them. Follow official evacuation routes, not shortcuts, since roads may be damaged or blocked in ways that aren't visible. Tell someone outside the affected area where you are going if possible. Do not return home until authorities say it is safe — secondary hazards (aftershocks, unstable buildings, live wires, contaminated water) often persist after the initial event.
